name: Folliculitis shower hygiene (post-gym shower)

lead: Showering soon after exercise aims to give you fewer breakouts and bumps on the back, chest and shoulders.

The idea is to remove sweat, oil and surface bacteria that can irritate hair follicles. General references on acne mechanica, caused by heat, friction and pressure, suggest showering soon after exercise, though no controlled study was found.

paras: People rinse off right after training rather than sitting in sweaty clothes, and change out of the gym clothes. It is usually paired with clean clothing and sometimes a gentle cleanser.
No harms are described. General advice notes that over-washing or harsh cleansers can irritate skin.

chain: Less sweat and bacteria on skin
angle.text: Showering soon after sweating washes off sweat, oil and bacteria so back and chest follicles are less likely to get irritated, meaning fewer body breakouts. General references on acne mechanica suggest the habit.

lead: Showering soon after sweating is a hygiene habit people adopt to keep their back, chest and shoulders clear of body acne ("bacne") and folliculitis, the inflamed, pimple-like bumps that form around hair follicles. The payoff in looks is smoother, clearer skin on the torso and fewer marks or scars, which matters for shirtless and physique photos.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes folliculitis as inflammation of hair follicles, most often from Staphylococcus aureus, with friction from clothing, blocked follicles and shaving listed as triggers.[1] Its acne mechanica article describes acne triggered by friction, heat and pressure from tight clothing, straps or sports gear, notes that athletes are most affected, and lists showering soon after exercise, loose breathable clothing and keeping skin clean and moisturized as prevention.[2]
Lifters discuss bacne often on T Nation, usually in connection with training and supplements, with advice such as not scrubbing affected skin.[3]
infobox: Reduce sweat-related follicle irritation and body acne
Salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide cleansers (general references)

paras: Practitioners shower after workouts to remove sweat and oil, and change out of sweaty clothing. General references list cleansers with salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide as options, which may sting sensitive skin.[2]

Folliculitis occurs when a pathogen enters a follicle damaged by friction from clothing, blockage or shaving. Types include bacterial (most often Staphylococcus aureus), hot-tub folliculitis from Pseudomonas, fungal and Malassezia forms, Demodex mite folliculitis and non-infectious forms such as pseudofolliculitis barbae.[1] Wikipedia says most simple cases resolve on their own, with topical antiseptics or antibiotics used depending on type, and that cases can occasionally progress to cellulitis or abscess or recur.[1]

Acne mechanica is most common in athletes whose sweaty skin rubs against uniforms or equipment; men and people with a genetic tendency are described as more prone. Wikipedia notes it usually clears once friction and heat are avoided and pores stay clean, though scarring or discoloration can follow continued rubbing.[2]

No controlled study of post-exercise showering for preventing folliculitis was found. The prevention advice appears in general references on acne mechanica, which Wikipedia flags as needing better medical sourcing.[2]
On T Nation a poster advises against scrubbing bacne, saying scrubbing can open a sore and spread it, while other threads mention bacne in the context of supplements or steroid use.[3]
